Against the Right to Be Forgotten: A Defense of Unrestricted Access to Historical Online Information

Introduction

In 2014, the European Court of Justice handed down its landmark decision in Google Spain SL v. Agencia Española de Protección de Datos, establishing what has come to be known as the "Right to be Forgotten" (RTBF). The ruling determined that individuals could compel search engines to delist links to information about them that was "inadequate, irrelevant, or no longer relevant." Since then, this principle has been codified in Article 17 of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and has inspired similar legislative efforts across the globe. Proponents celebrate these laws as essential protections for individual privacy and personal reinvention. However, beneath the appealing rhetoric of second chances and digital dignity lies a legal framework that fundamentally threatens freedom of expression, historical integrity, public accountability, and the epistemic foundations of democratic society. The Right to be Forgotten is, at its core, a privatization of censorship—an instrument that allows individuals to rewrite the public record to suit their personal interests, often at the direct expense of the public good. This essay argues strongly against RTBF laws and in favor of unrestricted access to historical online information, opposing any legal mechanism for the removal of publicly available past records.

I. The Right to be Forgotten is Censorship by Another Name

The most fundamental objection to RTBF laws is that they constitute a form of censorship, regardless of how they are rhetorically packaged. When an individual successfully petitions to have information about themselves delisted or removed from public access, the practical effect is indistinguishable from state-sponsored suppression of information. The fact that the original information may remain technically available on an obscure webpage does not meaningfully mitigate this concern. In the modern information ecosystem, a piece of information that cannot be found through a search engine effectively does not exist for the vast majority of users. Delisting is de facto deletion.

Free expression, as enshrined in the First Amendment to the United States Constitution, Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and countless other legal and philosophical frameworks, encompasses not merely the right to speak but the right to hear, to read, to access, and to know. When someone exercises the "Right to be Forgotten," they are not merely asserting control over their own narrative—they are actively preventing others from accessing truthful, legally published information. This is not a privacy right in any traditional sense. Privacy concerns the protection of information that has not yet entered the public domain. Once information has been lawfully published—whether through court records, news reports, or other legitimate channels—it has become part of the shared informational commons. Allowing individuals to retroactively withdraw truthful public information from accessible circulation is a power that, in any other context, we would recognize immediately as censorship.

The philosopher John Stuart Mill argued in On Liberty that the suppression of any opinion or fact is a "peculiar evil" because it "robs the human race." Mill's harm principle acknowledged that liberty could be curtailed to prevent direct harm to others, but he drew a sharp line at the suppression of true information. The Right to be Forgotten does not merely suppress opinions; it suppresses facts—verified, published, legally obtained facts. If we accept the premise that individuals can compel the removal of truthful information about themselves from public access, we have accepted a principle that can be, and inevitably will be, expanded in dangerous directions.

II. Historical Integrity and the Preservation of the Public Record

Human civilization depends on the preservation of records. The entire discipline of history rests on the premise that the past can be examined, interrogated, and understood through the documents and accounts that survive. Libraries, archives, and—in the modern era—digital repositories serve as the collective memory of humanity. The Right to be Forgotten strikes directly at this foundation.

Consider the implications if RTBF principles had been available throughout history. Could Richard Nixon have petitioned to have records of Watergate delisted? Could the executives of Enron have demanded the erasure of news articles documenting their fraud? Could politicians who made racist speeches in their youth demand that those speeches be rendered unfindable? The answer, under a robust interpretation of RTBF laws, is potentially yes—and this should alarm anyone who values historical truth.

Defenders of RTBF laws argue that the legislation typically includes exceptions for matters of public interest, but this distinction is far less clear and far less protective than proponents suggest. The determination of what constitutes "public interest" is inevitably subjective, politically contingent, and susceptible to manipulation. In practice, RTBF requests are often adjudicated by private companies—search engines like Google—that have neither the expertise nor the institutional mandate to make nuanced determinations about the historical significance of information. Google's own transparency reports reveal that it has granted approximately 47% of all RTBF requests since 2014, affecting millions of URLs. Each delisted link represents a piece of the historical record rendered invisible—not because it was false, defamatory, or illegally obtained, but because someone found it personally inconvenient.

The digital age has democratized access to historical information in ways that previous generations could scarcely imagine. Court records, newspaper archives, public filings, and countless other documents that were once accessible only to those with the resources and knowledge to visit physical archives are now available to anyone with an internet connection. This democratization is one of the great achievements of the information age. RTBF laws threaten to reverse this achievement, creating a fragmented and unreliable public record in which the information available to the public is determined not by its truthfulness or relevance but by the willingness of its subjects to litigate.

III. The Chilling Effect on Journalism and Public Discourse

Journalism serves as the immune system of democratic society. Investigative reporters uncover corruption, hold the powerful accountable, and provide citizens with the information they need to make informed decisions about governance and public life. RTBF laws pose a direct and severe threat to this function.

When individuals can compel the delisting of news articles, investigative reports, and other journalistic works, the practical effect is to undermine the entire enterprise of accountability journalism. A journalist who spends months investigating a corrupt official, a fraudulent business, or a dangerous organization may see the fruits of their labor rendered invisible by a simple RTBF request filed years after publication. The knowledge that this can happen creates a profound chilling effect. Why invest the time, resources, and personal risk required for serious investigative journalism if the subjects of your investigation can simply erase your work from the searchable internet?

This chilling effect extends beyond professional journalism to public discourse more broadly. Bloggers, citizen journalists, activists, and ordinary individuals who share truthful information about matters of public concern are all vulnerable to having their contributions to the public record suppressed. In an era when democratic institutions face unprecedented threats from disinformation and declining public trust, the last thing we should be doing is creating legal mechanisms that make truthful information harder to find.

The case of a Spanish man, Mario Costeja González, whose RTBF complaint launched the entire legal framework, is instructive. Costeja González sought to have delisted a 1998 newspaper announcement about the forced sale of his property to recover social security debts. The information was true. It was legally published. It was a matter of public record. Yet the European Court of Justice determined that his personal interest in having this information rendered unfindable outweighed the public's interest in accessing it. This precedent effectively establishes that an individual's desire for a curated personal reputation can trump the public's right to access truthful information—a principle that is fundamentally incompatible with the values underlying a free press.

IV. The Asymmetry of Power and the Protection of the Privileged

One of the great ironies of RTBF laws is that they are marketed as protections for ordinary individuals against the overwhelming power of technology companies, yet in practice they disproportionately benefit the wealthy, the powerful, and the well-connected—precisely those who least need legal protection and who have the most to gain from suppressing information about their past conduct.

Filing RTBF requests, navigating appeals processes, and—when necessary—litigating in court requires resources, sophistication, and legal representation that are not equally distributed across society. Wealthy individuals and corporations can hire reputation management firms and legal teams to systematically scrub the internet of unflattering information. Ordinary citizens, by contrast, often lack the knowledge, resources, or confidence to exercise these rights effectively. The result is a system that serves as a reputation laundering service for the privileged while doing little for those who genuinely need protection from online harassment or privacy violations.

Consider the types of individuals who are most motivated to invoke RTBF laws: disgraced executives seeking to rehabilitate their professional reputations, politicians hoping to bury evidence of past scandals, convicted criminals seeking to conceal their histories from future employers and associates, and public figures whose past statements or actions have become inconvenient. These are not sympathetic cases of vulnerable individuals being victimized by the internet; they are cases of powerful actors seeking to manipulate the public record to serve their private interests.

The asymmetry of power in RTBF enforcement is further exacerbated by the fact that the targets of delisting requests—search engines—have strong commercial incentives to comply rather than resist. For Google or Bing, the cost of fighting an individual RTBF request is almost always greater than the cost of simply granting it. This creates a systematic bias toward deletion, as search engines rationally choose to delist first and ask questions later. The public, which has no seat at the table in these proceedings, bears the cost of this lost information.

V. The Impossibility of Consistent Application

RTBF laws suffer from a fundamental problem of administrability: they require case-by-case determinations that are inherently subjective, inconsistent, and resistant to principled application. The core question—whether information is "inadequate, irrelevant, or no longer relevant"—is not one that admits of objective answers. What is irrelevant to one person may be critically important to another. Information that seems outdated today may become newly significant tomorrow. The passage of time does not necessarily diminish the relevance of information; in many cases, it enhances it.

Consider a business executive who was involved in a financial scandal twenty years ago. Under RTBF principles, the passage of time might be considered a factor weighing in favor of delisting. But what if that executive is now seeking investors for a new venture? What if they are being considered for a position of public trust? The information about their past conduct is not less relevant because it is old—it is potentially more relevant because of the executive's current activities. Yet under RTBF laws, the executive may already have succeeded in having this information rendered unfindable, depriving potential investors, employers, and the public of information that is directly material to their decisions.

The problem of consistency is compounded when RTBF principles are applied across jurisdictions. The internet is global, but RTBF laws are national or regional. Information that is delisted in Europe remains accessible in the United States, creating a patchwork of information availability that is both practically unworkable and philosophically incoherent. Either information is relevant to the public record or it is not; its relevance cannot coherently change based on the geographic location of the person seeking it. Yet this is precisely the situation that RTBF laws create, Balkanizing the internet and undermining the universal access to information that is the internet's most transformative feature.

VI. Existing Legal Frameworks Are Sufficient

Proponents of RTBF laws argue that they are necessary to protect individuals from the unique harms of the digital age—the persistence of online information, the ease of access, and the potential for outdated information to cause ongoing reputational damage. These concerns are not trivial, but they are already addressed by existing legal frameworks that do not require the wholesale suppression of truthful public information.

Defamation law provides robust protections against the publication and dissemination of false and damaging information. If information about an individual is untrue, they can seek its removal through defamation proceedings that include procedural protections for both parties and require a judicial determination of falsity. Unlike RTBF laws, defamation law targets false information specifically, preserving the public's access to truthful records.

Privacy law, including protections against the disclosure of private facts, the misappropriation of likeness, and intrusion upon seclusion, provides additional protections for individuals whose genuinely private information has been disclosed without consent. Data protection laws, including provisions of the GDPR beyond Article 17, regulate the collection, storage, and use of personal data in ways that protect individual privacy without requiring the suppression of truthful public information.

Where specific harms require targeted interventions—such as revenge pornography, doxxing, or the unauthorized disclosure of medical or financial records—legislatures can and should enact narrowly tailored laws that address these specific problems without creating a general right to suppress truthful public information. The Right to be Forgotten is a blunt instrument where a scalpel is needed, and its collateral damage to free expression, historical integrity, and public accountability far outweighs its marginal benefits over existing legal protections.

VII. The Slippery Slope is Not Hypothetical

Critics of slippery slope arguments often dismiss them as speculative, but in the case of RTBF laws, the slope is neither hypothetical nor gradual—it is empirical and accelerating. Since the 2014 Google Spain decision, the scope and ambition of RTBF laws have expanded dramatically. The European Commission initially proposed that RTBF delisting should apply only within the borders of the requesting jurisdiction, but subsequent litigation has pushed for global application—the idea that a delisting order issued in France or Germany should compel Google to remove results worldwide, including in countries with robust free speech protections that would never have countenanced such suppression.

In 2019, the European Court of Justice ruled in Google LLC v. CNIL that EU law does not require global delisting, but the question remains actively contested, and several national data protection authorities continue to push for extraterritorial application. If these efforts succeed, the RTBF will become a tool through which the most restrictive jurisdiction on earth can determine what information is available to users everywhere—a race to the bottom in which the country with the lowest tolerance for public information effectively sets the global standard.

The expansion is not limited to geographic scope. RTBF principles are being invoked in contexts far beyond their original application. Convicted criminals have sought to have news reports of their convictions delisted. Public officials have sought to suppress reporting on their official conduct. Religious organizations have sought to hide reports of institutional abuse. In each case, the logic of the RTBF provides a framework for suppression: the information is old, it is damaging, it is "no longer relevant." The public interest exceptions that are supposed to prevent these outcomes are interpreted narrowly and applied inconsistently, providing far less protection than proponents claim.

VIII. The Value of Uncomfortable Truths

At its philosophical core, the Right to be Forgotten reflects a deeply mistaken assumption: that individuals have a right to control how others perceive them, and that this right extends to suppressing truthful information that might lead to unfavorable judgments. This assumption is incompatible with the foundational values of liberal democracy.

In a free society, individuals are entitled to form their own opinions based on available information. They are entitled to decide for themselves whom to trust, whom to do business with, whom to vote for, and whom to associate with. These decisions depend on access to information—including unflattering information, outdated information, and information that the subjects would prefer to suppress. The Right to be Forgotten substitutes the judgment of the individual subject for the judgment of the public, determining unilaterally that certain information should not be available for others to consider.

There is, moreover, genuine social value in the persistence of uncomfortable truths. The knowledge that past actions will remain part of the accessible public record serves as a powerful deterrent against misconduct. If individuals know that their fraudulent business practices, their ethical violations, their criminal conduct, or their dishonest public statements will remain findable indefinitely, they have a strong incentive to behave responsibly. The Right to be Forgotten weakens this incentive by promising that the consequences of past actions can be escaped through legal process rather than through genuine reform and accountability.

IX. The Alternative: Transparency, Context, and Digital Literacy

Rather than suppressing information, societies should invest in tools and education that help individuals and institutions navigate the abundance of online information responsibly. Digital literacy programs can help people evaluate the relevance and significance of historical information, understanding that a decades-old bankruptcy does not necessarily reflect an individual's current financial reliability, and that a youthful indiscretion does not necessarily define an adult's character. Contextual labeling and annotation—allowing individuals to add context or responses to information about themselves without suppressing it—respects both the individual's interest in fair representation and the public's interest in access to truthful information.

Employers, landlords, and other decision-makers can be educated—and where necessary, regulated—to consider the age, context, and relevance of information rather than mechanically penalizing individuals for decades-old records. Some jurisdictions have already enacted "ban the box" laws that prevent employers from asking about criminal history on initial job applications, addressing the legitimate concern about the lasting impact of criminal records without suppressing the underlying information from the public record.

These approaches preserve the integrity of the public record while addressing the legitimate concerns that motivate RTBF advocacy. They represent a mature and nuanced response to the challenges of the digital age, in contrast to the blunt censorship of the Right to be Forgotten.

Conclusion

The Right to be Forgotten is predicated on a seductive but ultimately dangerous premise: that the discomfort caused by the persistence of truthful information justifies its suppression. In a world of perfect actors and perfect adjudicators, perhaps such a system could be made to work without significant harm. But we do not live in such a world. We live in a world where the powerful exploit every available tool to evade accountability, where the line between public interest and private embarrassment is contested and unclear, where the entities charged with adjudicating these questions—private corporations—have neither the mandate nor the incentive to protect public access to information, and where the expansion of censorship tools follows a predictable and well-documented trajectory from limited exception to broad suppression.

The answer to the challenges posed by persistent online information is not less information but better information—more context, more literacy, more understanding, and more respect for the public's fundamental right to know. Freedom of expression and access to information are not luxuries to be sacrificed at the altar of personal convenience; they are the foundations upon which democratic self-governance, historical understanding, and individual autonomy rest. The Right to be Forgotten, however well-intentioned, undermines these foundations, and it should be opposed by everyone who values truth, transparency, and the integrity of the public record.

The past belongs to all of us. No individual, no corporation, and no government should have the power to erase it.

By Staff Writer, The Modest Proposal Gazette

In a bold new frontier for human progress, a growing movement of brave souls has decided that the solution to life's embarrassing moments isn't growth, accountability, or a self-deprecating sense of humor — it's demanding the entire internet develop amnesia on command.

A Proud Historical Tradition

Critics have noted that the impulse to scrub inconvenient records has a rich and storied pedigree. Soviet photo editors were, in many ways, the original pioneers of the "right to be forgotten," painstakingly airbrushing disgraced officials out of photographs with the kind of meticulous craft that today's advocates can only dream of achieving with a GDPR request form.

"We stand on the shoulders of giants," admitted no one in the movement, because admitting that would be historically literate and therefore unhelpful.

Of course, comparing a European privacy regulation to Stalinist purges is wildly overdramatic. The Logistics of Forgetting

The practical challenges are staggering and therefore hilarious.

Under current implementations, Google doesn't actually delete information — it simply de-indexes certain results in certain jurisdictions. This means your regrettable 2013 op-ed titled "Why Bitcoin Is a Fad" still exists in its full glory; it's just harder for your French colleagues to find it. Your British colleagues, post-Brexit, are operating under a whole different regulatory framework and may or may not be laughing at you right now. Schrödinger's Embarrassment.

"It's like putting a Post-it note over a billboard," explained one data rights researcher. "The billboard is still there. Everyone on the other side of the street can still see it. But you feel better, and isn't that what law is for?"

The EU's system also requires someone — usually an underpaid content moderator or an algorithm with the moral reasoning capacity of a particularly confident toaster — to decide which information the public has a legitimate interest in and which information is just, like, really bumming somebody out.

This is a power we previously reserved for newspaper editors, historians, and your mom deciding which photos to put in the family album. ("We don't need to show Kevin's first wife, dear. That chapter is closed.")

The Slippery Slope Greased With Good Intentions

Now, in fairness — and I am contractually obligated by the rules of satire to include a moment of fairness — the "Right to be Forgotten" advocates aren't entirely wrong about everything. There are genuine cases that tug at the heartstrings: revenge porn victims, rehabilitated offenders who served their time, minors whose youthful idiocy was immortalized before their prefrontal cortex finished buffering.

These are real problems deserving real solutions, which is precisely why it's so entertaining to watch the concept get enthusiastically adopted by:

  • A surgeon who would prefer you not Google that malpractice settlement
  • A company whose environmental record reads like a horror novel
  • A politician whose prior policy positions are "no longer reflective of their current values" (their current values being: winning)

The movement's most charming quality is its sincere belief that the right tool for all of these wildly different problems is the same blunt instrument: making search engines pretend things didn't happen.

Supporters insist this is fundamentally a privacy issue, not a censorship issue. And they have a point — in the same way that boarding up the windows of a library is fundamentally an architecture issue, not a literacy issue.

The distinction, we are told, is that censorship is when the government suppresses information it doesn't like, whereas the Right to be Forgotten is when individuals use government-mandated legal frameworks to suppress information they don't like. See? Completely different. One has more forms.

"Information wants to be free," the old internet saying goes. To which the Right to be Forgotten crowd responds: "And I want information to be free to disappear quietly, like my college roommate who owes me $300."

A Modest Counter-Proposal

Rather than erasing the past, perhaps we could simply normalize having one. Imagine a world where a job interviewer finds your old blog posts and says, "Ah, you were once a nineteen-year-old with bad opinions. As was I. As were we all. Radical concept, I know. It would put a lot of privacy lawyers out of work. But consider the alternative: a world where every public figure, every company, and eventually every person with enough resources can curate reality like an Instagram feed — all blemishes smoothed, all inconvenient chapters deleted, all accountability quietly de-indexed.

We'd end up with a gleaming, searchable internet full of nothing but the versions of ourselves we want to project. A digital world of pure, pristine, unverifiable fiction.

Come to think of it, we might already be there.

When a corrupt official embezzles millions from a school district, and a local journalist spends months documenting every transaction, every lie, every betrayal of public trust — should that official, five years later, have the right to make that reporting disappear? Should they be able to approach a search engine and say, "This is inconvenient for me. Remove it"?

When a corporation poisons a water supply and the court records, the news articles, the testimony of affected families are indexed and searchable — should that corporation be able to clean its digital slate and present itself to the next community as a trustworthy neighbor?

When a predator is documented, when a fraud is exposed, when a powerful person's actions are laid bare by the courage of witnesses and reporters — should the passage of time alone grant them the power of erasure?

Because that is not privacy. That is sanitization. And history teaches us — screams at us — that sanitized history is the first tool of the oppressor.

Consider what we are really discussing.

Every civilization that has burned books, every regime that has rewritten textbooks, every authority that has scrubbed archives — they all believed they had good reasons. They all had justifications. The information was "dangerous." It was "outdated." It was "harmful." It "didn't represent who we are anymore."

The language of the Right to be Forgotten is disturbingly fluent in this same vocabulary.

Now, I want to be fair. The architects of these policies are not tyrants. Many of them are responding to real pain — the woman whose decade-old mistake dominates her search results, the reformed individual who cannot escape a youthful conviction. I do not dismiss that pain. It is real, and it deserves compassion.

But compassion does not require amnesia. And the solution to individual suffering cannot be the dismantling of collective memory.

Let's talk about what we lose.

We lose journalism. Not immediately — but slowly, insidiously. When any article can be de-indexed, when any report can be rendered effectively invisible, you don't need to censor the press. You simply make their work disappear after the fact. The journalist still wrote it. It still technically exists. But if no one can find it, does it functionally exist at all?

We lose historical research. Scholars of the future will encounter a digital record full of holes — not because information was never created, but because it was deliberately removed. They will study a version of our era that has been curated not by historians, but by the subjects of history themselves. Imagine studying Watergate if Nixon had the right to be forgotten. Imagine understanding the financial crisis if every banker involved could scrub their names from the record.

We lose accountability. This is the most fundamental loss, and it is irreversible. Accountability requires memory. Democracy requires accountability. Therefore, democracy requires memory. This is not a philosophical abstraction. This is a logical chain, and if you break any link, the whole structure collapses.

And let's be honest about who actually benefits.

The Right to be Forgotten is marketed as a shield for the vulnerable. But in practice — in documented, observable practice — it becomes a weapon of the powerful. It is politicians who file removal requests about unflattering coverage. It is executives who want bankruptcy filings hidden. It is public figures who want their records cleaned.

The ordinary person with a embarrassing photo? They rarely have the legal resources, the sophistication, or the persistence to navigate these systems. But the powerful? They have armies of lawyers ready to exploit every provision.

We are building a tool we are told will protect the weak, but it is being wielded by the strong. And every time we expand its reach, we hand more power to those who already have the most to hide.

Now, I know what the counter-argument sounds like.

"But people change! Should someone be defined forever by their worst moment?"

No. Of course not. But the answer to that question is more information, not less. The answer is context. The answer is the ability to add to the record — to say, "Yes, this happened, and here is what I did afterward. Here is how I grew. Here is who I am now."

That is a narrative of redemption. That is a genuine second chance. Deleting the past isn't growth — it's denial. And a society that institutionalizes denial is a society building on sand.

The most powerful stories of transformation in human history — from the confessions of Augustine to the testimony of reformed criminals who now mentor youth — derive their power precisely because the past is acknowledged, not because it is erased.

Let's also confront the practical reality.

Information, once created, does not truly disappear. It migrates. It replicates. It lives in screenshots, in archives, in the memories of those who read it. The Right to be Forgotten doesn't actually make anyone forget. It creates a false sense of erasure while the information persists in less regulated, less contextualized, less accountable spaces.

So what have we actually accomplished? We've removed the information from the places where it was most likely to be accurate — established news outlets, court records, verified databases — and driven those seeking it to rumor, to speculation, to the dark corners of the internet where context goes to die.

We haven't protected anyone. We've just made the truth harder to verify and easier to distort.

There is something else that troubles me deeply.

Who decides? Who is the arbiter of what deserves to be remembered and what deserves to be forgotten? A judge? A bureaucrat? An algorithm designed by a private corporation?

Every one of these options should terrify you.

Because the power to decide what is remembered is the power to decide what is real. And no single entity — no government, no court, no company — should hold that power. The moment we accept that some authority can determine which truths are accessible and which are not, we have abandoned the foundational premise of an open society.

We have, in the most literal sense, outsourced reality.

My friends, I understand the impulse.

The internet can be cruel. Digital permanence can feel like a prison. And the desire to start fresh is as human as breathing.

But the answer is not to give anyone — anyone — the keys to the archive. The answer is to build a culture that values context over condemnation. A culture that reads beyond headlines. A culture that understands that people are more than their worst searchable moment.

The answer is more humanity, not less information.

Because once you establish the principle that inconvenient truths can be made to vanish — once you create the legal and technical infrastructure for selective forgetting — you have built a machine. And that machine will not remain in the hands of the sympathetic. It never does. It will be captured by those with the most to gain from your ignorance.

So here is what I am asking of you.

Defend the record. Defend it fiercely, even when it's uncomfortable. Especially when it's uncomfortable. Because the uncomfortable parts are precisely the parts someone wants you to forget.

Demand transparency over erasure. Demand context over deletion. Demand that the answer to bad information is better information, not no information.

Stand against the seductive, dangerous, historically catastrophic idea that we can build a better future by selectively demolishing the past.

The right to know is not a luxury. It is not a privilege to be balanced against convenience. It is the bedrock of every free society that has ever existed. And every society that has surrendered it has learned — too late, always too late — what grows in the darkness of chosen ignorance.

We are the first generation to have the ability to record everything.

Let us not also be the first generation foolish enough to throw it away.

Thank you.
